summary: Extends the performance measurement method of RFC 6374, which measures packet loss and delay on Label Switched Paths, using Synonymous Flow Labels. It broadens the technique from MPLS-TP flows to generic MPLS LSPs, including multipoint-to-point and similar cases.

plainLanguage.summary: To check how many packets get lost, you color-code them and count at both ends. This extends that trick to more kinds of network paths.

questions: what is a synonymous flow label
how does mpls packet loss measurement work
subtitle: Counting lost packets and measuring delay on MPLS paths by tagging batches of traffic with synonymous labels.

tldr.problem: RFC 6374 measures packet loss and delay using the measurement message itself as the counting boundary, which causes accounting errors with multipath, multiple cores and long forwarding pipelines, and it does not identify the source on multipoint-to-point paths.
tldr.mechanism: Packets are grouped into batches, each marked with its own Synonymous Flow Label (SFL). The receiver counts per batch, and new message types report delay as time buckets, summary statistics or average arrival time.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6374 measurements now work on generic MPLS LSPs, including multipoint-to-point ones, not just MPLS-TP. Combined loss and delay measurement using SFLs is explicitly not supported by this document.

today: RFC 9571 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2024, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 6374 and the RFC 8957 SFL framework.

sections.title: Why Batches Instead of Query Packets
sections.content:
RFC 6374 defined loss and delay measurement as an Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) protocol for MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) LSPs, which only support point-to-point and point-to-multipoint paths. This RFC extends it to generic MPLS and adds more sophisticated measurements for both cases.

RFC 6374 uses the loss measurement message as the demarcation point for counting packets, and RFC 8372 explains why that can produce significant errors. With Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP), packets can arrive out of order relative to the measurement packet, or on different hardware interfaces. Even without ECMP, processing can be spread over several cores, link aggregation can cause synchronization issues, and some forwarders have a long pipeline between handling a packet and incrementing its counter.

The remedy, described in RFC 9341, is to batch packets at the sender and mark each batch so the receiver can recognize neighbouring batches. On a multipoint-to-point LSP there is a further problem: MPLS packets carry no source address, so source-specific information is needed to identify batches from one source. RFC 8957 supplies the tool, Synonymous Flow Labels (SFLs), labels that mimic the behaviour of other labels and so act as batch identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: If you count mail only when a special note arrives, bundles that took different routes get mixed up. Putting a sticker on each bundle fixes this because you count by sticker.

sections.title: Loss Measurement with SFLs
sections.content:
The data service packets of the flow being measured are grouped into batches, and every packet in a batch carries the SFL for that batch. The sender counts how many packets are in the batch. Once it is confident that all of them will have arrived, it sends a Query message using the same SFL as the batch, to learn how many were actually received. The difference is the number lost.

The Query and Response formats are described in the section on carrying packets over an LSP with an SFL.
sections.plainLanguage: You send a bundle of 10 letters with a red sticker, then ask the other end how many red-sticker letters arrived. If they say 9, you know one got lost.

sections.title: Delay Measurement with SFLs
sections.content:
A single-packet delay measurement, as in RFC 6374, times one packet across the LSP. It does not normally need an SFL, because delay should depend on the Traffic Class bits. But if SFLs are already used for loss measurement, or label-inferred scheduling is in use, the SFL is REQUIRED, so that the probe packet sees a delay representative of real data packets.

To measure many packets without sending many probes, a batch of real data packets is marked for delay. Loss and delay batches can overlap in time, so the RFC walks through four cases. In each, an SFL marked for delay (D) is synonymous with the loss SFL (A), which is synonymous with the underlying Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC). A D packet is therefore counted in the A loss batch and in the delay statistics, and is forwarded as normal. Whether it is counted twice or the counters are reconciled when reporting is a local matter.

When delay packets straddle a loss batch boundary, they must be treated as part of batch A or batch B, and the Query must wait until all the packets have arrived. To take several delay measurements inside one loss batch, two delay SFLs (C and D) are used alternately.
sections.plainLanguage: Some stickers mean count me, and a few special ones mean count me and time me too. Special packets still travel like all the others, so the timing is honest.

sections.title: Simplifying Rules
sections.content:
Allowing every combination of loss, delay and overlapping batches would make configuration, testing and implementation complex and costly. The RFC therefore states default rules:

  • Any system that needs to measure delay MUST be able to measure loss, and MUST be configured to measure loss. Whether the loss statistics are collected is a local matter.
  • A delay measurement MAY start at any point during a loss batch, but its interval MUST be short enough to finish before the enclosing loss batch completes.
  • The second delay batch (D) must last long enough that all packets of the first (C) have been received before it completes. This holds when the time to send a batch is long compared to network propagation time, a parameter the operator can set.

Since the sender controls the start and duration of both kinds of batch, these rules can be implemented in the control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: To keep things from getting tangled, the rules say that if you time packets you must also count them, and a timing round has to finish before the counting round ends.

sections.title: Richer Delay Statistics
sections.content:
Three new methods go beyond RFC 6374. Each places different demands on the packet forwarder, and the operator picks one to suit the diagnosis needed.

Time buckets. The receiver measures the gap between packets, sorts it into delay buckets and counts packets per bucket. For example, buckets for up to 1 microsecond, 2, 4 and 8 microseconds, and over 8, make five buckets. This shows more structure in jitter than a simple average and avoids a per-packet multiply, but the bucket intervals probably need to be programmable.

Classic standard deviation. The responder reports the number of packets (n), the sum of delays (S), the maximum and minimum delay, and the sum of squares of inter-packet delay (SumS). These give the mean, the outliers and, through var = (SumS - S*S/n)/(n-1), the variance of the inter-packet gap. The RFC notes a concern that SumS and S*S/n can be similar when variance is low, but accepts the method because it needs no division in hardware.

Average delay. Following RFC 9341, the responder returns the sum of arrival timestamps and their count, or the time of the first and last packet and the count, or both. The latter allows average delay to be found at several points along the path. The RFC also allows sampled measurement, where only a packet at the start of a marked group is measured, which avoids ECMP effects. Recording the gap for every packet pair is outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one stopwatch time, you can keep score in boxes (fast, medium, slow), or keep a running total, the fastest and slowest, or just note the first and last arrival.

sections.title: Carrying Messages with an SFL
sections.content:
A measurement packet uses the same MPLS label stack as the data packets being measured, with the LSP label and then the SFL, plus a Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) so the receiver can tell OAM packets from data. An Associated Channel Header (ACH) type field says what is measured; for MPLS Direct Loss Measurement it is 0x000A. The new delay messages use their own ACH types.

The measurement message can have three parts. The fixed-format portion travels in the ACH channel. An optional SFL TLV reminds the receiver which SFL carried the message, which matters because many MPLS implementations do not give the label stack to the OAM handler; it is required when messages go over UDP and MUST be included unless the responder is known not to need it. Optional Return Information tells the responder where to send the response; it MUST be carried unless the response is requested in band on a point-to-point LSP.

The SFL TLV holds an SFL Batch identifier, an SFL Index, the SFL itself (a label as in RFC 3032) and the FEC that was used to request it. Having both the SFL and the FEC plus index supports several implementation types. The RFC states that combined loss and delay measurement using SFLs is not currently supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The test packet wears the same outfit as normal packets, plus a small badge saying I am a test, so it travels the same road and gets the same treatment.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
Putting source or flow information in a packet gives more identity information and can degrade privacy. SFLs do not specifically name the originating node, except by inspecting the network at the point of ingress or the control protocol packets. The RFC suggests mitigating the threat by encrypting control protocol packets, changing the synonymous labels regularly, and using several labels concurrently.

The security considerations of RFC 6374 and RFC 8372 apply, and the privacy issue is treated as a security consideration. There are no other new security issues for the MPLS data plane, and any control protocol that requests SFLs must check the request is legitimate. An attacker who corrupts the SFL TLV could disrupt measurements in a way the responder cannot detect, but the RFC expects the operator to notice anomalous results and considers the attack extremely unlikely under normal MPLS security practice.
sections.plainLanguage: Stickers that show where a bundle came from could tell a snoop too much, so you change the stickers often and keep the notes secret.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content:
IANA allocated three values in the MPLS Generalized Associated Channel (G-ACh) Types registry for the new messages: 0x0010 Time Bucket Jitter Measurement, 0x0011 Multi-packet Delay Measurement and 0x0012 Average Delay Measurement.

It also allocated Type 4, Synonymous Flow Label, from the 0-127 range of the MPLS Loss/Delay Measurement TLV Object registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The number office gave each new kind of test message its own ticket number so nobody mixes them up.
